LeafMachine3 · experiment

Leaf bilateral symmetry

How symmetric is each leaf lamina about its own midvein, which measurements capture that, and can symmetry be used to pick out clean, archetypal masks? Measured on the tip-up Leaf_Oriented silhouettes so left and right mean the same thing for every leaf.

What the numbers say
  • Measuring against the traced midvein instead of a straight chord drops median SIA from 0.151 to 0.142 (6% lower) and raises median Dice from 0.857 to 0.895. That difference is not biology — it is the published straight-axis methods charging a curved midvein as asymmetry.
  • The chord axis reports MORE asymmetry than the midvein axis for 62% of leaves (median ΔSIA = +0.016, max +0.523).
  • Midvein sinuosity predicts that penalty (Spearman ρ = +0.47, p = 4.0e-07, n = 105): the more curved the midvein, the more a straight-chord method overstates asymmetry.
  • The composite archetype score tracks SIA at Spearman ρ = -0.97 — on this cohort it is almost entirely the symmetry term. That is a property of the data, not a flaw in the score: the independent quality terms saturate at 1.0 for most leaves (integrity 94%, completeness 99%, trace 76%), because these masks are already structurally clean. Symmetry is the only signal that varies here, so it does the ranking by default — and the galleries are the check on whether a low-symmetry leaf is a bad mask or simply an asymmetric leaf.
  • 2 leaf(s) have |A*| > 0.4 — one half more than 2.3× the other, which is not a real simple-leaf shape. Their worst midvein keypoint confidence is 0.37 against 0.94 for everything else, and their median Dice is 0.39. These are midvein trace failures, not asymmetric leaves — the pose model ran the midvein along a margin, so the lamina ended up almost entirely on one side. Across the whole cohort Dice and worst-keypoint confidence correlate at Spearman ρ = +0.32. So the most immediately useful application of these metrics may not be mask QC at all: they are a cheap, automatic detector for bad landmark traces, which matters while the pose model is still alpha.

Method

Every leaf is measured in the oriented frame, so “left” and “right” mean the same thing for every leaf in the cohort. The Reporter's Leaf_Oriented masks are produced by a crop → rotate → content-fit chain; the landmarks live in whole-sheet coordinates, so that chain is replayed exactly on the keypoints. The rebuilt silhouette matches the saved PNG at IoU 1.000000, which is what guarantees the midvein really lies on the mask it is measuring.

Two axes are then built from tip to base:

chord : the straight lamina_base → lamina_tip line — what Shi et al. and Wang et al. must use midvein : lamina_tip, midvein_0..14, lamina_base — smoothing-spline fitted, resampled to equal arclength

Each axis induces a curvilinear coordinate system on the mask: s is normalized arclength (0 at the tip, 1 at the base) and u is the signed perpendicular offset, positive to the viewer's left. Equal-arclength strips drawn perpendicular to a curved axis would overlap on the inside of a bend and leave gaps on the outside, so instead each lamina pixel is assigned to its nearest point on the axis. That is a Voronoi partition of the polyline: it tiles the lamina exactly once, with no overlap and no gaps, and the per-strip areas therefore sum back to the total lamina area exactly — a property that is asserted in the tests.

The lamina used is the hole-filled silhouette: the question is whether the outline mirrors, and insect or decay holes are damage to a leaf that grew at its full size. Hole area is measured separately and fed to the quality score instead. For the whole-shape overlap measures the two halves are reflected after straightening into (s, u) — reflecting across a single Euclidean line would count a curved midvein as asymmetry, which is precisely the artifact this experiment is trying to isolate.

The metrics

Every metric below is computed twice per leaf — once against the straight chord, once against the traced midvein. n = number of arclength strips.

Area, from paired strips

ARAR = ΣALi / ΣARi
Shi et al. 2018
Total left:right area ratio. Simple and comparable to the literature, but blind to localized asymmetry — a bulge on the left near the tip cancels a bulge on the right near the base and AR still reads 1.0.
A*A* = (AL − AR) / (AL + AR)
signed, bounded
The same information as AR but bounded to [−1, 1] and signed: positive means the viewer's left half is larger. Bounded means it can be averaged across a cohort without one extreme leaf dominating.
SIASIA = (1/n) Σ |ALi − ARi| / (ALi + ARi)
Shi et al. 2018
The paper's headline index: mean proportional disagreement between paired strips. Catches local mismatch that AR cancels away. Every strip counts equally, so a sliver of lamina at the very tip carries the same weight as the widest part of the blade.
WSIAWSIA = Σ|ALi − ARi| / Σ(ALi + ARi)
area-weighted
The area-weighted counterpart of SIA, and the closest thing here to a directly interpretable “what fraction of the leaf fails to mirror”. Read it as a lower bound on the symmetric-difference fraction, not as equal to it: summing |ALi−ARi| collapses the distribution of lamina within each strip, so it equals the true symmetric difference only when the two halves of every strip nest perfectly. The Dice/SD family below measures the real overlap.
DSIADSIA = (1/n) Σ (ALi − ARi) / (ALi + ARi)
signed strip mean
Mean directional bias. Read it against SIA: SI high with DSI ≈ 0 means large differences that alternate sides; SI ≈ |DSI| means one side is consistently larger.
RMSEARMSEA = √( (1/n) Σ(ALi − ARi)² )
Shi et al. 2018
Unstandardized, so it grows with leaf size. Included for comparability with the literature; prefer SI/WSI when comparing leaves of different sizes.

Half-width profiles

MAEw / RMSEw / NRMSEwNRMSEw = √( mean( ((wL−wR)/(wL+wR))² ) )
margin envelope
Distance between the two half-width profiles. The normalized form is scale-free. Widths here are the margin envelope (max |u| on that side), which is what a caliper measures — not area/Δs, which differs for a lobed leaf with a deep sinus.
rwrw = corr( wL(s), wR(s) )
profile shape
Whether the two sides expand and contract at the same longitudinal positions, independent of how large those expansions are. RMSE and rw are complementary: a leaf can have well-aligned lobes of unequal size (high r, high RMSE) or equal-sized lobes in the wrong places (low r, moderate RMSE).

Whole-shape overlap

Dice / IoU / SDDice = 2|L′ ∩ R′| / (|L′| + |R′|)  ·  SD = 1 − Dice
whole-shape overlap
The two halves straightened into (s, u) coordinates, the right one reflected, then overlapped. This is the only family that accounts for the entire outline at once rather than a reduction to strips. Reflection happens after straightening, so a curved midvein does not count as asymmetry.
HausdorffH = max{ supx∈L′ infy∈R′ d(x,y),  supy∈R′ infx∈L′ d(x,y) }
worst-case margin
Sensitive to a single unmatched lobe or tear, where the mean measures stay low. That makes it the natural detector for one-off segmentation damage as opposed to gentle overall lopsidedness.
DcDc = √( (s̄L−s̄R)² + (ūL−ūR)² )
half centroids
Separates longitudinal displacement of area (one half's mass sits nearer the base) from lateral extent (one half reaches further from the midvein). Two leaves with identical SIA can differ entirely in which of those is happening.

Where the asymmetry sits

C(s), Cmax, ICC(sk) = Σi≤k(ALi − ARi) / (AL + AR)
cumulative
The running signed imbalance from tip to base. Its endpoint is A*, but the path is the information: two leaves can both end at zero, one by staying balanced throughout and the other by cancelling a left-heavy apex against a right-heavy base.
apex / mid / base thirdsSIapex = mean|a(s)| for s ∈ [0, ⅓]
where it happens
Localizes the disagreement. s = 0 is the tip and s = 1 the base. Apex asymmetry often means a damaged or folded tip; basal asymmetry is frequently genuine biology (oblique-based leaves) or a petiole-junction segmentation artifact.

The axis itself

sinuosity, Dm, KmSm = Lmidvein / Dbase,tip
midvein geometry
How far the traced midvein departs from a straight chord: arclength ratio, maximum perpendicular deviation, and total absolute turning. These are the cause of the chord-vs-midvein gap below, so they predict which leaves the literature's straight-axis method will misjudge.
ΔQaxisΔQaxis = Qchord − Qmidvein
the LM3-only measurement
Every metric computed twice — once against the straight base→tip chord the published methods must use, once against the actual traced midvein. The difference is apparent asymmetry that is really just a curved midvein. No silhouette-only method can measure this.

Straight chord vs. traced midvein

The measurement LM3 can make that a silhouette-only method cannot.

Why this is the interesting panel. Shi et al. (2018), Wang et al. (2018) and Guo et al. (2020) all divide the lamina with a straight base→apex line, because a silhouette is all they have. LM3 traces the midvein, so the same leaf can be measured both ways and the difference attributed. A leaf whose midvein bows is penalized twice by the chord method: once because the chord cuts across the blade, and again because the strips perpendicular to it are no longer perpendicular to the leaf. The most affected leaf is YPM_1038926111_Bignoniaceae_Catalpa_purpurea#54: SIA 0.922 on the chord vs 0.399 on the midvein, with sinuosity 1.0521.

Cohort distributions

Which metrics are redundant?

How to use this. Metrics inside a near-1 block are measuring the same thing; keeping all of them just triple-counts one signal in any downstream score. The families worth keeping are the ones that stay uncorrelated: a strip-based magnitude (SIA or WSIA), a whole-shape overlap (Dice), a worst-case term (Hausdorff), a positional term (rw or Dc), and the axis geometry (sinuosity). AR is deliberately included to show the failure the 2018 paper warns about: it can sit near 1.0 while the local indices are large. Two blocks are redundant by construction and are kept only as a check that the matrix is behaving: Dice and IoU are a deterministic reparameterization of each other (IoU = Dice/(2−Dice)), so they must show ρ = 1.00; and WSIA tracks SIA at ρ ≈ 0.95 because they differ only in weighting. Sinuosity, by contrast, is nearly uncorrelated with every symmetry metric — it is independent information, which is exactly why it predicts the chord-vs-midvein gap above rather than the asymmetry itself.

Taylor's power law

Read this one skeptically. Wang et al. (2018) fit log VD = log α + β log MD across leaves; β is a cohort parameter, not a per-leaf score. On raw pixel² areas this cohort gives β = 1.99 (R² = 0.90, n = 105) — but that is very nearly an arithmetic identity rather than a result. Di has units of area, so scaling a leaf up by k multiplies MD by k² and VD by k⁴, forcing β → 2 for any cohort of similar shapes at different sizes. Here log MD correlates r = 0.90 with log lamina area, so the raw fit is largely measuring how big the leaves are. Refitting on the size-normalized differences di = |ALi−ARi|/(ALi+ARi) gives β = 1.59 (R² = 0.70, n = 105) — that is the number with the size effect removed, and the one worth interpreting.

Do symmetry metrics find archetypal leaves?

usable — 96 exemplar — 90 vetoed — 9 click any point
click a point to inspect a leaf
left half right half midvein axis chord axis
Click any point to see that leaf's oriented mask with its two halves tinted and both candidate axes drawn — every leaf in the cohort is clickable, not just the ones in the galleries below. That left-hand view is the fastest way to tell the three failure modes apart: a green midvein axis running down the middle with unequal halves is a genuinely asymmetric leaf; a green axis hugging one margin is a bad landmark trace; a ragged or multi-part silhouette is a bad mask.

The three tiers. Vetoed leaves had a score term driven to zero by a structural fault (extra components, holes, truncation, an unusable midvein trace) — these are the only hard rejects. Usable is everything else. Ringed points are exemplars: usable AND above the score cut, which is a policy knob (--min-score), not a measurement. The structural gates apply at every threshold; only the score cut moves.

Honest reading. The archetype score deliberately combines symmetry with independent mask-quality evidence (stray-component fraction, truncation, convexity, landmark-trace confidence) as a weighted geometric mean, so any one bad term vetoes a leaf. Holes are excluded from both the gates and the score: the shape under test is the holes-filled silhouette, so an insect hole is not part of the outline being measured. The raw component count is excluded too — it vetoes single-pixel specks — and replaced by the fraction of area outside the main blob.

And the honest result: this scatter is a tight monotone band. On a cohort whose masks are already structurally clean, the other three terms saturate at 1.0 for most leaves, so the composite is very nearly the symmetry term alone. That is a fact about this data, not a validation of the score — the independent terms would only start separating leaves on a messier sweep. Treat the weights and thresholds as a first proposal to be tuned against the galleries below, not as established values.

Least archetypal

Lowest composite score. There are three different causes in here and the panels tell them apart: a genuinely messy mask (stray blobs, torn margin); a genuinely asymmetric leaf (oblique base — normal in many taxa, and the score is wrong to penalize it); and a failed midvein trace, which shows up unmistakably as the green axis running along a margin instead of down the middle, with nearly all the lamina on one side. Read the left panel of each before trusting the score.

Limitations & caveats
  • The midvein comes from an alpha pose model. Where the trace is wrong, the midvein axis is wrong, and the leaf will look asymmetric for a reason that has nothing to do with the leaf. Landmark confidence is carried into the score for exactly this reason, but a confidently wrong trace is not detectable here.
  • “Left” is the viewer's left of the oriented mask. It is not a botanical anodic/cathodic call, so the directional-asymmetry literature (Chitwood et al. 2012; Martinez et al. 2016) cannot be tested with these signs — a cohort mean near zero is expected even if strong directional asymmetry exists, because the sheet orientation is arbitrary.
  • A leaf can be genuinely, biologically asymmetric (oblique bases are normal in many taxa) and still have a perfect mask. Low symmetry is evidence of a messy mask only in combination with the independent quality diagnostics; the galleries are there to check that combination by eye.
  • Fluctuating-asymmetry interpretation is deliberately avoided. Májeková et al. (2024) reviewed 51 studies and found leaf FA is not a reliable stress indicator, so nothing here should be read as an environmental signal.
  • The cohort is small and taxonomically narrow. Thresholds tuned on it will not transfer unexamined to a broad herbarium sweep.

Left = the viewer's left of the tip-up oriented mask, which is consistent across leaves precisely because every mask is oriented; it is not a botanical adaxial/abaxial or anodic/cathodic call, so a cohort-mean signed imbalance near zero is expected even where real directional asymmetry exists.
